newsitem.title: ITALY: FEATURE - Italy's banks look to change, but only slowly.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Italy's banks look to change, but only slowly.

text.p: The wheels of change are slowly creaking into action in Italy's bureaucratic banking world. Often criticised as overcrowded, overmanned, and over-expensive for customers, the long-awaited restructuring may be starting.

The immediate pressure for change is coming as Italy's fragmented banking system suffers from rising non-performing loans, or bad debts, while banks have seen interest income sliding as Italian interest rates continue to decline.
But long-term structural problems still remain in an Italian market of 900-plus different banking groups bedevilled by high labour costs, complex customer charges and the state's stranglehold.

With some large international banks now eyeing Italy, many banking industry analysts have stressed the need for the Italian banking system to get its house in order -- to restructure, modernise, consolidate and privatise.

Official pressure is also rising as Italy realises the need for its banks to compete with big northern European banks as cross-border barriers come down and Europe moves closer towards Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio has urged banks to cut their labour and management costs, and Prime Minister Romano Prodi with Treasury Minister Carlo Azelgio Ciampi appear to share Fazio's concern about Italy's outmoded banking system.

Fazio is reported to have stressed that lay-offs should concern at least 10 percent of Italy's bank personnel, estimated at around 30,000 employees, and banks now seem more willing to risk union anger at cutting their bloated workforces.
BANKS CONSIDERING CHANGE

So now, after many false dawns, Italy's largest banks seem to be stirring into action and looking to privatise, consider or undertake mergers while they see interest in their own shares from some big U.S. investment funds.
"We are on the verge of something substantial and by the end of 1997 we are likely to see a lot of changes," said banking analyst Francesco Ricciulli at Milan brokers Pasfin.
Ricciulli sees Italian banks moving to improve their lending portfolios, cutting costs and increasing the commission income they earn from businesses like fund management.

Traditionally, Italian banks have relied heavily on interest income or the spread between borrowing and lending rates. But as Italian interest rates have fallen to the lowest level for nearly 22 years, so banking profit margins have been squeezed.
CATALYST FOR CONSOLIDATION

The spark for change came with the Italian Treasury's blessing for nationalised Banca Nazionale del Lavoro (BNL) and former state insurer INA to take over a 60 percent stake in ailing Banco di Napoli, which in 1995 recorded the largest ever loss in Italian banking history.

Analysts point out that some Treasury help must have been behind the merger of the woefully badly-managed Naples-based bank and BNL with its large workforce, thus giving both the chance to rationalise and produce a stronger single unit.

This could just be the catalyst for consolidation in an industry where the top seven banks have around 35 percent of the banking market, compared with other European countries like Britain which have a more rationalised system with fewer bank groups.
"Italian banks lack global players and this is inconsistent with the size of the Italian economy," said banking analyst Derek Chambers at investment bank HSBC James Capel.
STRING OF RATIONALISATION MOVES

Only this month, Italy's largest savings bank Cariplo, already looking to privatisation this year, made a formal approach to Banco Ambrosiano Veneto about a strategic alliance -- which could lead to a merger and create Italy's largest bank.

Some analysts pointed out that Milan-based Cariplo's acquisition record, especially in the south of Italy, has been poor, while Ambroveneto has been more circumspect and shied away from taking over the troubled Banco di Napoli.

Ambroveneto is 29 percent owned by French Credit Agricole and so could give the merged group an international flavour. Although Ambroveneto is clearly Cariplo's favoured partner, analysts say a further possible partner could be another northern bank, Banca Commerciale Italiana (BCI).

Meanwhile, Italy's largest bank San Paolo di Torino has put privatisation on the fast track as its foundation, which controls 65 percent of its shares, wants to put a further 45 percent on the market very soon this year.

Large U.S. funds have been attracted by the revival of interest in banking groups. Chase Nominees bought 2.06 percent of Credito Italiano and raised its stake in investment bank IMI to 3.06 percent from 2.03 percent, while Fidelity bought 3.1 percent of Credito to become one of its biggest shareholders.
Ironically, Italy's earlier attempt at privatising banks was seen as a partial failure as Credito and BCI fell under the influence of investment bank Mediobanca and allies.

Credito was the first bank owned by state holding IRI to be privatised in December 1993, followed by BCI in March 1994. A limit of three percent was set for individual shareholders which could only be abolished after three years with a group extraordinary meeting.
Mediobanca maintained its control by using its allies to hold small stakes, but as the three-year rule may be voted down soon Credito's share price has soared as stakes change hands.

On privatisations Mediobanca has it own ideas. Its chairman Francesco Cingano said the government should transfer to the Treasury as it did with telecoms holding STET, Italy's main five banks Cariplo, Banca di Roma, BNL, Montepaschi and San Paolo and then start privatising them.
